description:
Hi! I'm an LLM Engineer with a background in Biomedical Sciences, currently pursuing an MSc in Health Data Science.

For this challenge, I'd love to build something useful around astronaut health monitoring, combining AI, data analysis, and an intuitive dashboard.

I'm looking for star teammates with an interest in coding, design, space science, or data visualization. All experience levels are welcome!

Let's build something we're proud of!
summary:
RESOLVE is a working prototype that helps astronauts collect and review fatigue-related health observations when time, equipment and communication are limited. It combines sleep history, a fatigue self-report, contextual observations and an experimental browser-based vigilance task in one guided workflow.

An explicit evidence policy checks whether observations are usable. A deterministic planner then recommends the next feasible check using available equipment and the remaining session allocation. If a workstation becomes unavailable, the workflow can switch to a tablet; if both are unavailable, it preserves the unresolved evidence gap in the human-review brief.

Built with NASA human-research and exploration-medicine resources, RESOLVE makes the collection process, missing evidence and handoff visible. It supports human review without producing a diagnosis. The prototype uses synthetic demonstration observations. Team-reported usability completion was 13/25 initially and 12/15 after revision, with small, mixed-exposure groups.
details:
An astronaut begins a health review. Some observations are already available, time is limited, and the workstation becomes unavailable halfway through. Which check can still be completed, and what must remain unresolved?

DiastiMed developed RESOLVE to make that situation understandable and actionable. Our working prototype addresses the astronaut health-monitoring challenge through a focused fatigue-and-alertness collection workflow.

HOW IT WORKS

RESOLVE brings together sleep history, a fatigue self-report, contextual observations and an experimental three-minute browser-based vigilance task. Each observation is assessed against an explicit evidence policy covering freshness, values, units, collection method and declared quality.

A deterministic planner uses the available evidence, equipment, prerequisites and remaining session allocation to recommend the next feasible check. Usable observations can be reused. When equipment availability changes, the plan is recalculated.

Our demonstration shows a workstation becoming unavailable and the workflow selecting a tablet alternative. When both devices are unavailable, RESOLVE preserves vigilance as unresolved in the review brief. Missing evidence remains visible throughout the handoff.

The final brief separates observations, limitations, unresolved evidence and the next collection step. A structured JSON export includes the inputs, policy, available task results and recorded workflow events so another person can inspect how the brief was produced.

NASA FOUNDATION

NASA resources on sleep-related risk, Standard Measures, psychomotor vigilance testing and exploration medical decision-support architecture informed the project’s focus and design. NASA imagery is credited separately.

These resources provide the research foundation; the prototype’s collection windows and task rules are provisional engineering assumptions. The browser task is PVT-inspired and has not been validated as equivalent to NASA’s instruments or a clinical assessment.

TECHNOLOGY AND ORIGINALITY

We built the application with React, TypeScript, Vite, HTML/CSS and native Canvas rendering, using browser storage for local session persistence. Source code, evidence documentation and development credits are publicly available on GitHub.

RESOLVE’s creative contribution is the connection between evidence quality, equipment availability, collection planning and an explicit handoff. Its decisions follow inspectable rules. No language model runs inside the application.

EVALUATION

The current release includes 33 automated tests and a reproducible benchmark of 256 synthetic planning scenarios. RESOLVE found complete feasible plans in 169 cases, matching the greedy comparator; the fixed-order comparator completed 167. Among the 167 cases completed by both RESOLVE and the fixed ordering, RESOLVE had lower declared cost in 15 and tied in 152, with zero median saving. These are model-based results, not measured crew-time benefits.

Additional sensitivity analysis covers 39,750 authored planning cases and 84 separate task-gate fixtures. It examines how decisions change with freshness windows, equipment, remaining allowance and assumed collection costs. The results demonstrate reproducible software behaviour without establishing medically correct settings or a general optimisation advantage.

An occupational health professional personally inspected RESOLVE and provided comments on the presentation of sleep, fatigue and workload information, visibility of unresolved evidence, and the human-review handoff. The team owner confirmed the inspection and authorship of these comments. This scoped review supports the assessment of workflow presentation and boundaries; it does not establish clinical validation, numerical-policy endorsement or measured participant comprehension. The review and its limitations are documented in the public repository.

INTENDED IMPACT

Following the scoped occupational-health review, the next steps are targeted review of numerical policy assumptions, browser-task and device calibration, and a prospectively documented comparison of handoff correctness, omissions, assistance and elapsed time..
